title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship
summary: Where Canadian rights come from, the fundamental freedoms and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the equality of women and men, the responsibilities that come with citizenship, and ways to serve and defend Canada.

sections.title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

blocks.text: Canadian citizens have rights and responsibilities. These come to us from our history, are secured by Canadian law, and reflect our shared traditions, identity and values.

Canadian law has several sources, including laws passed by Parliament and the provincial legislatures, English common law, the civil code of France and the unwritten constitution that we have inherited from Great Britain.

Together, these secure for Canadians an 800-year old tradition of ordered liberty, which dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in 1215 in England (also known as the Great Charter of Freedoms), including:

items: Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of speech and of the press;

blocks.text: Habeas corpus, the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state, comes from English common law.

The Constitution of Canada was amended in 1982 to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which begins with the words, “Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.” This phrase underlines the importance of religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person.
The Charter attempts to summarize fundamental freedoms while also setting out additional rights. The most important of these include:

items: Mobility Rights — Canadians can live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport.
Aboriginal Peoples’ Rights — The rights guaranteed in the Charter will not adversely affect any treaty or other rights or freedoms of Aboriginal peoples.
Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights — French and English have equal status in Parliament and throughout the government.
Multiculturalism — A fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity. Canadians celebrate the gift of one another’s presence and work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony.

sections.title: The Equality of Women and Men

blocks.text: In Canada, men and women are equal under the law. Canada’s openness and generosity do not extend to barbaric cultural practices that tolerate spousal abuse, “honour killings,” female genital mutilation, forced marriage or other gender-based violence. Those guilty of these crimes are severely punished under Canada’s criminal laws.

sections.title: Citizenship Responsibilities

blocks.text: In Canada, rights come with responsibilities. These include:

items: Obeying the law — One of Canada’s founding principles is the rule of law. Individuals and governments are regulated by laws and not by arbitrary actions. No person or group is above the law.

Taking responsibility for oneself and one’s family — Getting a job, taking care of one’s family and working hard in keeping with one’s abilities are important Canadian values. Work contributes to personal dignity and self-respect, and to Canada’s prosperity.
Serving on a jury — When called to do so, you are legally required to serve. Serving on a jury is a privilege that makes the justice system work as it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens.
Voting in elections — The right to vote comes with a responsibility to vote in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections.

Helping others in the community — Millions of volunteers freely donate their time to help others without pay—helping people in need, assisting at your child’s school, volunteering at a food bank or other charity, or encouraging newcomers to integrate. Volunteering is an excellent way to gain useful skills and develop friends and contacts.

Protecting and enjoying our heritage and environment — Every citizen has a role to play in avoiding waste and pollution while protecting Canada’s natural, cultural and architectural heritage for future generations.

sections.title: Defending Canada

blocks.text: There is no compulsory military service in Canada. However, serving in the regular Canadian Forces (navy, army and air force) is a noble way to contribute to Canada and an excellent career choice (www.forces.ca). You can serve in your local part-time navy, militia and air reserves and gain valuable experience, skills and contacts. Young people can learn discipline, responsibility and skills by getting involved in the cadets (www.cadets.ca).

You may also serve in the Coast Guard or emergency services in your community such as a police force or fire department. By helping to protect your community, you follow in the footsteps of Canadians before you who made sacrifices in the service of our country.

The civil code of France
The American Bill of Rights
The unwritten constitution inherited from Great Britain
quiz.why: The sources named are laws passed by Parliament and the provincial legislatures, English common law, the civil code of France and the unwritten constitution inherited from Great Britain.

quiz.q: Canada's tradition of ordered liberty dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in:
quiz.why: The booklet says the tradition "dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in 1215 in England".

quiz.q: Magna Carta is also known as:
choices: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
The Great Charter of Freedoms
The Constitution of Canada
The civil code of France
quiz.why: Magna Carta is "also known as the Great Charter of Freedoms".

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of the four fundamental freedoms?
choices: Freedom to own property
Freedom from taxation
Freedom of peaceful assembly
Freedom to bear arms
quiz.why: The four fundamental freedoms are freedom of conscience and religion; of thought, belief, opinion and expression; of peaceful assembly; and of association.

quiz.q: Freedom of speech and of the press is part of which fundamental freedom?
choices: Freedom of conscience and religion
Freedom of peaceful assembly
Freedom of association
Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression
quiz.why: The booklet lists "freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of speech and of the press".

quiz.q: What is habeas corpus?
choices: The right to enter and leave the country freely and apply for a passport
The right to vote in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections
The freedom of peaceful assembly and of association guaranteed to Canadians
The right to challenge unlawful detention by the state
quiz.why: "Habeas corpus, the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state, comes from English common law."

quiz.q: Habeas corpus comes from:
choices: The civil code of France
English common law
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Magna Carta
quiz.why: The booklet says habeas corpus "comes from English common law".

quiz.q: In what year was the Constitution of Canada amended to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
quiz.why: "The Constitution of Canada was amended in 1982 to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms."

quiz.q: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms begins with the words:
choices: "We the people of Canada..."
"I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful..."
"Canada is founded upon the principles of peace, order and good government..."
"Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law."
quiz.why: The Charter "begins with the words, 'Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.'"

quiz.q: The opening phrase of the Charter underlines the importance of:
choices: Religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person
The equal status of French and English in Parliament and throughout the government
Mobility rights, so that Canadians can live and work anywhere they choose in Canada
The 800-year old tradition of ordered liberty dating back to Magna Carta in 1215
quiz.why: "This phrase underlines the importance of religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person."

quiz.q: Which Charter right lets Canadians live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport?
choices: Multiculturalism
Official Language Rights
Mobility Rights
Aboriginal Peoples' Rights
quiz.why: The booklet defines Mobility Rights as the right to "live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport".

quiz.q: According to the Charter, what is the effect of the rights it guarantees on the treaty rights of Aboriginal peoples?
choices: They replace all treaty rights with the mobility and language rights set out in the Charter
They apply only to First Nations and do not extend to the Inuit or Métis peoples of Canada
They cancel any treaty rights not written into the Constitution when it was amended in 1982
They will not adversely affect any treaty or other rights or freedoms of Aboriginal peoples
quiz.why: "The rights guaranteed in the Charter will not adversely affect any treaty or other rights or freedoms of Aboriginal peoples."

quiz.q: Official Language Rights mean that French and English have equal status:
choices: Only in Quebec and New Brunswick
Only in the courts
In Parliament and throughout the government
Only in schools
quiz.why: "French and English have equal status in Parliament and throughout the government."

quiz.q: The Charter describes multiculturalism as:
choices: A policy introduced when the Constitution was amended in 1982
A responsibility of Parliament and the provincial legislatures
A fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity
A right that Canadians can exercise anywhere they choose in Canada
quiz.why: "Multiculturalism — A fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity."

quiz.q: Which of the following is listed among the most important rights set out in the Charter?
choices: Minority Language Educational Rights
The right to a free university education
The right to a guaranteed income
The right to own land
quiz.why: The Charter rights listed are Mobility Rights, Aboriginal Peoples' Rights, Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights, and Multiculturalism.

quiz.q: In Canada, men and women are:
choices: Equal under the law
Subject to different laws
Equal only in the workplace
Equal only in federal elections
quiz.why: "In Canada, men and women are equal under the law."

quiz.q: How does Canada treat barbaric cultural practices such as "honour killings," female genital mutilation and forced marriage?
choices: They are tolerated as part of multiculturalism
They are matters for the family to decide
Those guilty of these crimes are severely punished under Canada's criminal laws
They are dealt with only by provincial governments

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of the responsibilities of citizenship?
choices: Serving in the Canadian Forces
Serving on a jury
Learning both English and French
Owning a home
quiz.why: The responsibilities are obeying the law, taking responsibility for oneself and one's family, serving on a jury, voting in elections, helping others in the community, and protecting and enjoying our heritage and environment.

quiz.q: Which statement describes the rule of law, one of Canada's founding principles?
choices: Individuals and governments are regulated by laws and not by arbitrary actions; no person or group is above the law
Governments may act as they see fit in an emergency, since no law can bind the government itself
Elected officials are above the law because they are the ones who pass laws in Parliament and the legislatures
Laws regulate individuals but not governments, which may take arbitrary actions when they judge it necessary
quiz.why: "Individuals and governments are regulated by laws and not by arbitrary actions. No person or group is above the law."

quiz.q: When you are called to serve on a jury, you:
choices: May decline if you are busy
Are legally required to serve
Must pay a fee to be excused
Serve only if you are a lawyer

quiz.q: The right to vote comes with a responsibility to vote in:
choices: Federal elections only
Federal and provincial elections only
Federal, provincial or territorial and local elections
Local elections only
quiz.why: "The right to vote comes with a responsibility to vote in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections."

quiz.q: Why does the booklet say serving on a jury is a privilege?
choices: Jurors are paid a high salary, which contributes to personal dignity and to Canada's prosperity
It makes the justice system work, as it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens
Jurors choose the judges who settle disputes, and only citizens are allowed to take part
Only volunteers may serve, and volunteering is an excellent way to gain useful skills and contacts
quiz.why: "Serving on a jury is a privilege that makes the justice system work as it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens."

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of helping others in the community given in the booklet?
choices: Running for Parliament
Joining the Canadian Forces
Paying taxes
Volunteering at a food bank or other charity
quiz.why: The booklet lists "helping people in need, assisting at your child's school, volunteering at a food bank or other charity, or encouraging newcomers to integrate".

Conditions for voting
Charter rights

choices: Serving in the Coast Guard or the emergency services in your community, such as a fire department

Getting a job, taking care of one's family and working hard in keeping with one's abilities

quiz.q: Is there compulsory military service in Canada?
choices: Yes, for all citizens aged 18 to 25
Yes, for men only
No, there is no compulsory military service in Canada

choices: By joining a political party
By getting involved in the cadets
By serving on a jury
